claim: A linear/shallow classifier (SAPLMA) trained on an LLM's hidden-layer activations while it reads or generates a statement predicts the statement's truth value with 71-83% accuracy depending on base LLM, for both externally-provided and model-generated statements.
stance_target: internal hidden states encode correctness/truthfulness information not fully reflected in surface output
scope_conditions: General-domain true/false factual statements across six topics; whole-statement granularity; non-code
quoted_support: Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement... our trained classifier achieves an average of 71% to 83% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model.

claim: The LLM-assigned token/sentence probability is a weaker and confounded truthfulness signal (biased by sentence length and word frequency) compared to the hidden-state probe classifier.
stance_target: probes on hidden states are a more reliable correctness signal than naive model-output-derived signals (e.g. sequence probability)
quoted_support: while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness

claim: SAPLMA is the earliest widely-cited work establishing that a model's internal state, not just its output text or output probability, can reveal whether a generated or read statement is true, but it does not test code generation or per-requirement/per-claim decomposition of an answer.
stance_target: does prior latent-knowledge work already scoop per-requirement code-correctness probing?
scope_conditions: General NLP truthfulness only; whole-statement granularity; no code tasks
quoted_support: This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates.
